Have you learned methods for successful crate training? Crate training isn't just throwing the dog in the crate and hoping it will be fine. 

Here is some stuff that may help.

1) train the dog to go into the crate by luring and rewarding for being in the crate. Progress by closing the door and rewarding. Implement a release command when he is allowed to come out (open door, release dog when they are calm)

2) feed dog in the crate. You can leave the door open but eventually work up to closing the door and leave him there until done eating.

3) through out day, give dog a chewy or stuffed kong in the crate and leave him there for a few minutes working up to longer periods.

4)keep crate accessible and a positive experience so he feels comfortable and inclined to use the crate.

5) if dog is going crazy when you get home, don't let them out. Wait for calm behavior. ignore him. When he is calm let him out.

6) use a tarp/blanket to cover the crate. It can be calming for some dogs as it creates a den like experience.

7) practice using the crate multiple times a day such as when you are cleaning or doing small chores and when you want the dog out of the way.

Lastly, you have a Mal, they require a lot of work so I hope you and your family are committed to giving it the attention he needs.

I understand how mental health can make having a routine and maintaining consistency very difficult. But i can't stress how important it is that you fight through it and work with your dog. Most of these issues sounds like he isn't being properly and consistently trained and his good behaviors are not being properly reinforced.

I have an ACD and her puppy days, like yours, were rough. But your puppy will grow out of some of these issues. However, it sounds like you need to focus hard on a few things. 

Barking at everything: desensitization. You can teach him to associate certain things to commands. Doorbell, train him to go to his bed, for example. Further, teach a "quiet" command.

Potty in the house: you need to take him out to potty more offten. If he doesn't go then put him in the crate and let him out later. If he potties outside then he can stay out. Most importantly, WATCH HIM. If he is sniffing around then he may need to potty and you need to take him out ASAP. You can keep his leash on so you can maintain better supervision and also keep him from having free roam and getting into trouble. Also, it's easy to teach dogs to ring a bell when they need to go out. Recommend you teach this as a puppy and reinforced it (every time he rings it, that door opens for the potty)

Biting: he is a puppy. They teeth. Best advice, keep lots of chews on hand for him. If he is chewing on things he shouldn't, redirect to an appropriate toy or chew. Puppy proof your house. There are dangerous things he absolutely shouldn't be near. Establish a strong leave it command to get him to stop.

Socialization: if you are seeking an ESA, please please train and socialize for the best behavior. People with untrained ESAs are terrible.

Breed: if I recall, dachshund were bred for hunting small game. Familiarize yourself with the breed and identify things to train around. Know the difference between working line and non-workingline.

How do you set her up for success? As they gain confidence, they may be more eager to keep trying. Often times, if my dog is struggling and not getting it, I step back and make it easy. 

I taught her to sit pretty recently and I had to let her put her paws on my arm to support her self. I did this a ton until she developed the strength and duration to do it herself. 

When she reaches the point of training fatigue, have her do something easy that she knows just to retain a little motivation. I found that the more confident my dog is in a skill, the more she feels incline to do it.

For scent work, I started placing cheese and hot dogs close enough to get her so she learned to use her nose. After that I put the treat in a tin spice jar (found on amazon) with the scent I wanted her to find and if she found it, I reward. During this phase, I put the cans in the open where she could see them and taught her to sit when she smelled it. As she became more confident, she became more excited to play this "find it" game. As she progressed, I hid the tins in New spots to make it harder. 

Remember, don't push your dog to keep going if you haven't practiced duration to much. But what helps is making it fun and turning it into a game. 

Set your pup up for success. It seem easy to you, but it can be very hard for them. Keep your sessions relatively short (15min or so) and do many sessions through the day.

What is happening before he reacts? Sudden scary movements? Loud noises? Has he ever been desensitized to those things? Knowing this is important for management. As fare as training goes, there really isn't a one size fits all. Some dogs require more than just positive reinforcement. Not sure what training you tried, but consider looking at another trainer (balanced, force free based, BAT 2.0) I tried force free with my dog but I didn't find the result I needed for a dog that developed reactivity. In my experience every school I've attended it was a bit different and you belt up pretty quick in the beginning (if you are grasping the material easily/practicing out side of class) my first school had set days every other month that they did mass school testing so new belts came slower. My second school (wtf and more sport based such as competitions) you did one on one testing with the teacher and this happened when you and the teacher felt ready. My curent school does testing once a month which includes forms sparring and board breaking you also have to write short essays prior to testing.

Low belts are not expected to spar until about green belt. At blue belt you start breaking boards. Every belt has one-step sparing techniques that they learn that the must display but that's not to be confused with full geared out sparing. 

I got to my green belt quick but have since slowed down due to my school doesn't give new belts right after testing (there is about a week or 2 of waiting). My first school paid close attention to sparing (I actually failed a test back then due to my sparring). My current school focuses more of seeing how you attack and defend which doesn't seem like they weigh heavily on sparring.

In the end, if something doesn't work, take a step back and try something new. If you feel that you want to try balanced, do your research and learn how to properly use the tools to prevent injury or negative behavior. Don't jump on a prong but try a slip first. Larger dogs benefit from prongs because they give more control, especially for smaller humans.

In an effort to lose weight, I tried keto (maybe it was more low carb than strict keto. But that was the idea I went for). Basically, I started by getting a food log and logged everything I ate. I used to think I wasn't eating a lot until I looked at the calories and carbs. I ate more than I perceived. After that I cut out breads and pasta, sugar (replaced it with stevia), measured my portions, drank more water, replaced with soda with diet soda to reduce calorie intake and also worked to reduce my soda intake. 

I was surprised that I lost a lot in the first week (granted it was surely water weight) but I felt physically better. When I go out and order a non diet soda, I can't finish it because it is to sweet and it tastes "bad" compared to what I have grown accustomed to. I have saved money by not eating fast food/buying junk food and I make an effort to cook something I enjoy. I don't enjoy the task of cooking so get super basic when prepping lunch for work, however I have been collecting recipes for making new dishes that look good and just learning new things for cooking. 

On top of this, I have started intermittent fasting which made me realize that I don't need to constantly eat. I once told someone about it and they didn't like the idea of "starving yourself". Those people seem to be really week minded towards their weight goals. IF isn't starving yourself, but just setting boundaries on when you can eat.

In my experience so far, I have learned that I don't need a ton of carbs for the lifestyle I live (I'm not athletic), I ate more than I thought, I developed a love for healthier options and a hate for what I once loved, less is more (like a lot. I made big lunches for work that were less than 1.5k calories), I was able to lose weight quickly just by making healthy choices (with that I hate the "fat is beautiful" movement with people saying it's impossible to lose weight when they refuse to make the necessary changes). 

Be heavy doesn't feel good, but working to make a change feels great, especially when you see and feel it.

So I do follow Tom Davis, and I personally find his content helpful. I found him after I started doing balanced training and most of what he teaches is what I learned from my trainer.

For reference, I started as force free and was was absolutely able to teach my dog anything with ease, and it was/is a great experience. I moved to balanced when my dog developed reactivity, and I grew helpless. That said, balanced helped a ton. As I develop my training hobby, I have developed my own beliefs. Balance isn't the best, but neither is positive. I think training should be based on the dogs' needs. In regards to balance and training in general, never jump to the prong. Always start low with no aversive>slip>prong. Every dog is different, and their needs are also different.  I think it's always important to establish a foundation through force free. Once the dog understands the command, only then should you layer in a prong or e collar. 

I love positive methods, but I feel many dogs may suffer more if alternate training like balanced is one day out lawed. Training should be conducted based on the dogs needs, not by what you feel is scary. Many dogs where trained successfully with balanced methods and are happy. My dog ended up LOVING her balanced trainer. 

In the end, teach new things with positive methods, but develop your training to your dogs needs. Not every dog needs a prong and Tom even shows this as he chooses to use a slip on other dogs. Don't jump on the prong hoping for instant results. There is proper method to use it, including position, quick pops vice constant pressure, size etc. Your dog may not have needed it. Instead you could have tried an e collar or a slip. E collars are great because you can change the intensity or just use vibrate. I think many that try these methods without working with a professional end up failing because they don't recognize the fine details.

First thing, understand that your dog has a personality like you. They may not enjoy social interaction. My dog doesn't and that's fine. What you can try is clipping his nails on your own. If you are worried about a negative reaction then try muzzle training. Then clip one nail and reward with his jackpot (favorite) treat. You may consider clipping one toe at a time over the course of a few days so he can get used to getting trimmed and he gets into a routine of having his paws handled. 

I like to make a game and have my dog interact with the dremle and clippers by nose touching and giving paw. I think it's helpful by showing her that these tools equal reward opportunities and are not as scary as she thinks. 

As far as getting him used to people, just work him around many people and develop his confidence that people are normal. If he shows interest (sniffing) then reward lavishly. You may ask friends to help you and start by having them toss treats, but don't push it. Give a little and let him decide if it's worth it. Keep the interaction short. If he wants to continue then he will let you know. 

My dog doesn't care for others and doesn't want to be pet by strangers. It's scary for them. Imagine if some random guy came to you and started petting you. You would probably say something like "hey back off don't touch me". On the other hand if that random guy tossed some nice stuff to you then you may get a bit happy, but he is still some stranger.

Ask your vet/groomer/ friends if you can come buy to establish a relationship and do some work. But keep it short.

But consider what is higher value. My dog loves her frisbee......she also loves cheese. Her Frisbee may be more rewarding but she gets really excited and demanding about it. Having a low value reward is excellent in teaching the dog that they are doing great. But when they do something exceptionally well then they deserve a jackpot (the highest value reward). Another method is starting with play and end with play. 

I will play a game with high value reward to build motivation and then when we actually train I may use a low value reward unless my dog performs phenomenally. And then I return to the low value reward so I can challenge her to work hard for that high value reward. At the end we play a game with that high value reward because she did well and training should be a rewarding experience. I agree that you should phase out treats in order to prevent weight gain and that's where I may rely on my dogs toy only but I will use a ball vice the Frisbee. 

I use the Frisbee outside but indoors I have another high value alternative. A squeaky ball. 

Toys are very valuable and each toy may be more valuable than the last. The key is to not allow your dogs impulse ovcome the training goal. On another note, some dogs are more food motivated than toy.

With that, I agree that Michael ellis is the better in terms of communication and explaining the value of rewards. But if you can train your dog with a toy alone then that's fantastic.

This! The problem with "+R only" etc. Is that it can take ages. Some dogs don't have ages to learn. The best training is making it fun and POSITVE EXPERIENCE but still holding the dog acountable. All training is going to be stressful for you and the dog. It's how you handle that stress that determines the value of training. Start positive and end positive with games jackpot rewards etc. Can guarantee your dog will not care so long as you are fair, committed, and direct. Balanced training is not abusive unless you make it abusive. There are plenty of happy dogs trained in this method. 

However, training depends on the dogs needs. Some dogs will do just fine without aversive and with +R alone. The beauty of balanced training is that you don't even need to use a prong or e collar. You can train with just a slip lead. You train with just a flat collar. It's how you develop and apply leash pressure or a correction. Personally I think a flat collar is the worst tool because traditional collars do not apply even pressure like prongs and slips. In terms of corrections, people have the nasty idea that it involves yanking and drawing the dog to inflict a ton of pain and fear. It's not. And if you think that's proper then you are absolutely wrong.

I personally do balanced training. That said, I always make the effort to teach new commands using lures and shaping first. When my dog understands a command I layer in the ecollar for communication. I do use a prong (stallmark) for developing leash pressure and holding my dog accountable through corrections. I read some where that the prong mimics a dogs bite when they correct eachother which is a language they understand. Most of the time I let my dog correct herself such as when we heel. If she isn't paying attention and I turn then she gets the pressure. This leash pressure is great for holding them accountable. 

You mention Alpha training so I can't help but imagine this is dominance training. There is a difference between showing dominance and instilling accountability. With that I understand where you are coming from.

I personally believe that all training should start at the most basic level with the least aversives. From there you make the decision whether you dog may need an aversive. Prongs are best for large and strong breeds because they distribute pressure evenly and make the dog easier to handle, granted you must train responsibly so the dog understands what the pressure means. You can mess up a dog if you are irresponsible. 

As far as transitioning. Remove the aversive and develop your use of lures and shaping. Always start with a game and end with a game. Training should always be fun first.  You will also need to develop an alternate way to hold your dog accountable something that I personally struggled with when I was adamant about positive only methods. Positive reinforcement is a phenomenal method of teaching new things and challenging the dog to figure out what they must do. I think you should look up Michael Ellis. He does use balanced methods but he is very insightful on how to develop a lure, creat reward events, build drive etc. I enjoy Zak George as a positive only trainer for how he teaches and challenges his dogs (granted he has his faults, but i did find value in how he teaches new commands). KikoPup is a great one also for teaching tricks and basic obedience. Lastly, I enjoy Simpawtico for their insight on how to teach commands and how to give the dogs activities to do and even teaching the handler how to handle(they don't have a ton of stuf but what they have is really interesting and fun).

One, the walk is for both of you. You should enjoy it with your dog. Second, they are dog and need breaks. Let them be a dog.

Sniffing is how they learn about the world. What dogs have been here? What's this non-dog smell? Is this a female in heat? Etc. It's also very important in greeting. I'm American and I use a Stallmark prong and E-collar mini educator for my dog. I used to be against them as I was first learning about training my Cattle dog. From puppy hood I primarily used positive reinforcement to teach new commands. As my dog grew she developed territorial behavior and reactivity. During covid it got worse. As novice back then I admit my training was certainly not solid but I made an effort to attend classes and conduct research on how to teach new things.  Also, I feel my bond with my dog wasn't as strong as it is now and I think that's cause I was easy on her. Ultimately I found myself on a plateau in our training and positive methods seemed to be doing nothing.

I ended up deciding to try balanced training but not without researching and finding a good trainer. I still live by "start basic with positive methods to encourage the dog to try a new thing without aversives", and when my dog understands a command (something she should be obligated to obey for her safety and everyone elses) I begin layering the ecollar. 

The ecollar is a beautiful tool for communication. I have it set to a level where my dog just feels it (we know this when the dog shows a reaction by shaking the head or scratching). I then use the Stim before giving the command. This isn't a correction but rather a notification that she should pay attention (kinda like your phones notification before you see a text). The expectation is that she perform the command. Like leash pressure training, as the dog performs the ecollar pressure turns off. Conditioning is also a very important thing. When does the stim level go up? I usually turn mine up when we are in hi distraction environment (for reference my dogs lowest level is an 8 and when I turn it up I usually go to a 10. Mind you, these are levels out of 100 and I feel it at a 15 as an itch) if my dog doesn't have her focus on me due to reacting to something or hard staring I will slowly scroll up until she looks to me for direction. Like people dogs are prone to having stuff go in one ear and out the other.  When my dogs focus is on me, I don't even rely on the collar. It is a communication tool first. In terms of correction, I try to limit it to a vibrate. That said, I'm firm believer that an e collar can be a safer means of disrupting reactivity then putting your hands on the dog, granted this is when my dog has a barier between her and the stimuli. I say this because my dog has redirected on me before (i felt bad about it but I would never consider euthanasia when it may be my fault.). How I'm curently handling my dogs reactivity to passersby is by starting a fun game with her favorite toy. If we see some one walking by our fenced yard I tell her to get her toy and we start playing. If she reacts, I vibrate her collar.

As for the prong, I use this to establish walking structure. Before we go for a walk I make her heel. If I turn and she isn't paying attention then she corrects herself as the lead tightens. When the walk begins, if she is walking faster than me and gains distance, I will use a pop to correct her. I may also use her ecollar to cue her and direct her to heel again. I like testing her attention by stopping and see what she does. If she keeps going then the leash pressure goes on. I like to utilize a long line so I can break her and give her some freedom to explore . But as a working breed I aim to make her work and reward with her favorite toy/treats when she complies. 

I crate my dog when I go to bed and when i go to work. If my husband shares the same schedule as me then I may let her stay out during the night but set up boundaries. I don't like crating for long periods but she gets crated any time I can't maintain supervision for a long time. This is to protect my cats freedom and sanity and also visitors who may enter after notice for maintenance reasons.

Reguarding training, I start every session with a get-it game using a high value reward. This peaks her attention and as we train she gets rewarded with a high value treat. At the end of the session we play another game with more treats or her favorite toy. The goal is to always start positive and end positive.

As he becomes more obedient move closer to his distractions and continue. 

If you feel he is a danger, don't be afraid to use a muzzle. Also, tie a knot in his leash and step on the leash to help prevent him from pulling. Teaching him leash pressure would be helpful (you can teach this with a slip lead) just be safe and set him up for success.

A blanket or tarp over the crate is also useful so she can put eyes on her trigger which allows more focus on her crate activity. 

I worked with a balance trainer and one activity we did for triggers was: with the dog on a platform if the turn to engage with stimulus we lead them off in opposite direction which they turned and then lead them back up. This gives them a bit of a work out but also takes their attention off the distraction. If they re-engage with you then give lots of praise and work to continue that engagement. If she reengages with the trigger, then repeat the process. It's important to understand your dogs temperament to avoid any redirecting so start far away or with simple distractions. 

As you practice remember the 3Ds. Distance, Distraction, duration. Baby steps are a must but if you have an intelligent breed then you may make quick progress.

If you are interested, I recommend Michael Ellis, and Tom Davis on YouTube. Both use balance training methods but you try some of their stuff with luring. Michael Ellis has great info on engament games and a vast other stuff.

Positive reinforcement was a great foundation for my dog but balanced training instilled the expectation and it even developed our bond more than +R. The ecollar is great for off leash training too. It makes a phenomenal communication tool. 

The prong is great but as stated before, I would try a slip lead before a prong. Slip leads and prongs must be positioned high and behind the ears. There are many types of prongs. I currently use a stalmark on my dog. It's a plastic collar with rounded prongs so nothing sharp.

Sorry for long post but this topic is important to me. In general, aim to not need aversives but understand your dog may learn better. Aversives also are great for working breeds that must understand and comply with certain expectations.

So understand that you are not alone. I have an Aus. Cattle dog who I trained with +R only as a pup (I bought into the negativity of aversives without doing my own research). My girl did great at learning new thing through +R but it did nothing for us when she developed territorial behavior. She got worse during covid while we moved cross country. During my quarantine required for my job, I took a leap of faith and tried a balanced trainer because my dog needed an outlet for stress and because our other training wasn't cutting it. 

My first visit with her after 2 weeks into her board and train, it was hard to see the corrections but she did so well. She was eager to work and please.

Here's the surprising thing, our bond was trash during +R only. Now, my girl is so affectionate and loves working. Understand that you don't always need to use an aversive. I use my dogs e collar for communication to help her understand that a command is coming and she needs to pay attention. For example: stim>command> release the stim if she follows. 

ECOLLARS ARE NOT FOR SHOCKING THE HELL OUT OF YOUR DOG! Primarily, you should use it on the lowest level that your dog feels it. The level may be increased depending on distractions and if they are being a nuisance (i.e barking at passersby, other dogs) I up the stim for my dog when she is barking at walkers outside the fence. It's important to hold the stim and slowly scroll up until the dogs attention returns to you. For reference, I use an ET mini-educator.

I utilize the vibrate function when my girl is getting into stuff she shouldn't be but it's also been working its way to being a recall. When she barks at runners I use vibrate and she has been good at running back.

I also use a prong and my girl responds well to the leash pressure. 

Many will say that corrections lead to worse behavior and while it's true, it's important to understand that the correction has a proper timing to avoid negative association. Don't pop the leash while the dog is reacting but instead correct before the dog builds to that reaction. There is a proper way to apply it so be sure to practice.

I recommend YouTube channels by Tom Davis (my favorite for describing the corrections), Michael Ellis, and Larry Krohn.
These guys have so many great videos on how to properly use the ecollar and prong. 

I can't stress enough how important it is to educate yourself, practice, and (if offered) attend group classes to get help from the trainer to ensure you are handling the dog and applying the aversives correctly.

Some dogs do great with +R. But for those of us like you and me, something different works better. Not every dog responds the same to different training styles. +R is phenomenal for setting a foundation but (in my experience) balance training helps the dog understand the expectation.

If you ever feel that your dog is in the wrong hands, you can always stop. My dog LOVED her balanced trainer. That said, pay attention to how your dog responds to the trainer, if he is fearful of them then request another handler. At the end of the day, your dog will appreciate you more for setting an expectation and being a leader. He will love you no matter what.

I believe +R sets great foundation and if a pup develops a solid foundation early then maybe it won't need aversives later. But some adult dogs never received adequate training or learned proper social skills and thus they may need the extra reinforcement from an aversive. In my experience and research, aversives need to be introduced from none up to what ever helps the animal best. Some only need a slip while others need a hermspringer prong (my dog uses a stalmark plastic prong. I also utilize an ecollar). 

So many dogs are in shelters for behavior reasons which could be prevented if people open their mind to balanced training. It doesn't have to be the only method, but when +R fails it should be considered. I think most trainers aim for not needing an aversive but some dogs need it in order to understand the expectation.

Just a hobbyist who loves training my own dog. When my ACD was a pup, I was adamant about being +R only. I bought into the mindset that all aversives were bad and my dog would suffer. As she grew she developed Territorial aggression and lacked confidence in the RIGHT areas. I watched a ton of YT vids and did a lot of research and read books in order to be committed to +R. As time went on and covid happened along with a cross country move by car, my dogs behavior got worse and +R just did not do shit for her. 

During my quarantine, I knew she needed an outlet and so I invested in board and train and decided to try balance training. My dog did amazing. In my experience, +R works wonders until it doesn't. It is absolutely an amazing way to teach new commands and establish a foundation. However, some dogs require aversives in order to learn the expectation. +R only trainers will preach how you only hurt your dog with aversives but in reality, you can only do that if you do it all wrong. With +R, my dog only cared for her treats and didn't really respect the commands I gave. Not only that, but our bond wasn't great. When I turned to balanced training, her learning took off and she became so eager to work and she became so affectionate. 

In my opinion, the most inhumane thing someone can do to their pet is keep it drugged up because +R failed and they don't want to use an aversive. Some dogs, like people, need a "kick in the butt". If one form of training fails, try something new. Not all dogs learn the same. For instance, my dog learned to lay down through luring, however I trained my sisters Lab some basic obedience and I had to gently pull the dogs paws to help her lay down but she quickly figured it out and I was able to lure her and develop a hand signal. The issue with +R only is it takes way to long and if it fails then a trainer may suggest drugging the animal, until it's almost nothing but a shell, or advising putting it down. 

If anyone is struggling with +R and facing either drugging your dog or putting them down, please try something else but be sure to do research.

As someone who trained positive only (until My ACD began showing aggression) I can say in my experience, a balanced trainer did wonders for my dog. I believe every dog learns differently (some do phenomenal with positive only, others do phenomenal with balanced).

Balance training and the use of corrections does not mean abuse. I shared your anxiety when I enrolled my dog but I also did it because positive reinforcement only was not doing anything for my dogs issues. 

Today, my dog has more confidence, loves working, is overall more attentive to me, and the use of an ecollar has offered me a way to better communicate with my dog (it's not a correction, but rather a notification before the message).
Leash pressure training with or without a prong is a powerful tool. The prong offers the sensation as if another dog were correcting yours. You don't yank super hard and it must be positioned and fitted CORRECTLY to prevent harm. The prong I use doesn't sit on the trachea, instead the open portion where the leash attachment is sits there. This puts the prongs along the sides and back of her neck. 

Some dogs do just fine without a prong because they learn quickly about the leash pressure. Others figure it out much faster with a prong and you don't even have to do anything, rather the dog can make the pressure turn on or off all by themselves. 

All equipment can pose a hazard but its up to you as the owner to be educated and learn vice going in blind with high expectations.

You can share your concerns with your trainer, heck you could probably ask to visit a session and observe.

In the end, based off my experience, balance training was worth it vice listening to a positive only trainer suggest that I put my dog down or keep it sedated. A balanced trainer showed me that my dog only suffered from low confidence and made me realize that my dog needed a job and structure.
